utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina, Cermak, and Markac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I have three small issues. First, yesterday the -- Madam Registrar used a method of numbering in which a distinction was made between one Defence team or another Defence team. That was a mistake, as far as I understand. That means that exhibit numbers for the Defence start with D, then get a number, and that no distinction is made whether it is Gotovina Defence, whether it's Cermak Defence, whether it's Markac Defence. The cases are joined anyhow. So therefore the 1D1 and the 1D2 are now changed to D1, D2, D3. That's system as far as numbers are concerned. The second issue is that I invited the parties to consider whether where we yesterday admitted a number of exhibits under seal whether there was a need to do that. Is there any report on that? First of all, I'm addressing you, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. We haven't met with the Defence, but we looked at the exhibits and I can certainly say that P8, P9, P10, and P12 can be admitted openly, and we will look at the redactions of the remaining documents with the exception of the witness statements. There we need some more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Defence teams are invited, because I consider witness protection a shared responsibility, a shared duty, to see whether they agree that P8, P9, P10, and P12 could be unsealed. If so, if you please would have a look at it and then report after the first break if you are of a different opinion with the Prosecution. Then finally, and that's a matter for the witness. Witness 136, I received a message in which you inquired whether you would be given an opportunity to give a few further details on matters you thought it would assist the Chamber to have these details at the end of your testimony. Such an opportunity will be given to you. Then, Mr. Kehoe, are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just one matter. If there are additional details given, I certainly would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It goes without saying that if they are of -- of a certain substance and if they raise the need to put any further questions to the witness that of course you'll have an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. President and Your Honours. Good morning, ma'am. Madam Registrar, if we could put this is OTP 65 ter number 6492 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you intend to tender it, then perhaps you could ask already whether Madam Registrar would assign a number to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you assign a number to it because we will in fact tender it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D5 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could turn our attention to the second page of that document, and about halfway down on that second page you'll see "Urgent urgent urgent info." And if we could blow-up that particular area. Now, Madam Witness, if I may, under the "Urgent urgent urgent info," and this for the record is a document that was drafted by the UNMOs, United Nations Military Observers, of August the 4th at 1610 hours, 1995. You noted for us yesterday that your boyfriend came to the gate at approximately 1500 hours to see you. At number 1 in this, it notes that at 1515, and this is on the 4th, "Sector South headquarters is blockaded by ARSK. Anti-tank mines are laid on the main road to Knin - 100 metres from headquarters entrance gate." Now, Madam Witness, was your boyfriend a part of that mine-laying task by the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, definitely not. He came back from the positions carrying a wounded comrade. He was all covered in blood. He came to the town. We spent some 10 minutes there at the gate. A shell landed very close, and the security officer demanded that I go back into the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you observe the mines that had been laid out in front of the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on the ground there at the gate. I didn't have any time to look around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could just go into private session just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could go to this first page of this document which is now D5, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday, Mr. President, we referred to the issue at Podkonje, and I told Your Honour that I would present the basis of that if we look at paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "UNMO team Podkonje is not evacuated to headquarters yet. The APCs were threatened by ARSK forces. Negotiations are ongoing to get them out later on. As per the report at 1530, the Podkonje team is safe and sound in their location. HV authorities are already informed about the grid reference of the UNMO team locations. Shelling is ongoing in Knin. Gospic is reported to be under heavy shelling from 1525 hours." Now, yesterday, Madam Witness, you told the Trial Chamber that you knew nothing about the ARSK forces threatening the UNMO team at Podkonje on the 4th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, although I worked for them quite often at later stages, so I find it quite strange that they never told me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us shift back to some of the issues that we talked about yesterday, and I would like to direct your attention to one the clarification killings involved in the town of Knin and the individuals were Ilija and Mile Milivojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could you guide the Chamber always --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to the page and the numbers because searching for Podkonje in the yesterday transcripts doesn't help me out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I was going to do that, Judge, but I was just waiting for the translation to finish and it is statement 1. I believe that's -- 2, page 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you also refer to yesterday's testimony. There I'd like to have the page and line number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was just taking off where we left off from yesterday's testimony as opposed to referring back to a specific fact in yesterday's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted for us that you had gone to the area where Ilija and Mile Milivojevic lived on the 11th of August, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that these two individuals were dead with shotgun wounds to the head; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there to the house next door to find accommodation for the station of the UN military observers, and this woman reported to us that the body of a man was there. We immediately called the press office, the UN civilian police. I stood at the door, but I didn't go into the house because I was not feeling well. So I didn't see those two bodies myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just one correction. In the transcript it says "shotgun wounds" while the witness statement on page 7 says "gunshot wounds."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not exactly the same but it seems not to create great confusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, let me show you first the -- if we can pull up -- it is number 1D00302 to 1D00303.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it need a number, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D6 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And on the 6th person there it's Ilija Milivojevic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it has a certain identification number KN01/420. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to Exhibit 1D00299 to 301.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D7 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: First of all, the previous Exhibit D5 was not on the list of documents communicated to us. It's an OTP document so I don't have a problem. The second issue is if first before we discuss a document he just explain what it is and I also don't see an English translation of the previous document which is now D6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the document that we have at this juncture, which is in B/C/S. I think we -- it is readily apparent that this is a series of documents received by the UN concerning people who -- for which autopsies were performed. One of these two individuals, Ilija, number 6, Milivojevic, and we see the identification number of KN 01/420 matches up to the autopsy report that was provided by the Office of the Prosecutor, which is now marked for identification as D7. And we can see from that front page up in the left-hand corner, if we can bold that out in case number, please, the top of the page, we can see that the same case number is there matching up to the name of Ilija Milivojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear you are taking us to a list and now to an autopsy report. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we can -- you told the Office of the Prosecutor that these people had been shot in the head, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was standing there at the door of their house. I remember the stench of the decomposing bodies. I felt quite sick and I couldn't go in, but UN personnel were there and they told me what was inside, and they told me there was no need for me to go in at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us scroll down on that page for D7, for Ilija Milivojevic, and look at the cause of death. The cause of death written by the medical examiner was "It is my determination that the cause of death in case number KN01/420 was unascertained at autopsy."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you once again what I was told. I did not see the bodies myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can direct Your Honours to several paragraphs up in the summary, third paragraph down in the summary. It notes that: "The only antemortem injury identified to the bone was a single fracture of the left 10th rib lateral, without any special characteristics whatsoever. Its significance was uncertain. "In the absence of any soft tissues and any pathology or significant trauma, the cause of death remained undetermined. No other significant findings were made." Your Honour, we'll of course offer into evidence the D6 and D7. Of course we will provide a translation for that at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To be provided without delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would include also D5?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. That's an English original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then D5, D6, and D7 are admitted into evidence. D6 and D7 under the condition that shortly an English translation will be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could flip back to -- I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Madam Registrar, if we could flip back to D6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in D6, at the number 7, that is Milan Milivojevic, and identification number of KN01/421. Do you see that, Madam Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to -- and if I may, it is 1D00306 to 308.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D8 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, you can see again if we can go to that document and the identification number -- case number on the upper left-hand corner of this UN document it notes the case number KN01/421, which is the identification number for Milan Milivojevic in D6. Once again scrolling down to the cause of death. "Cause of death: It is my determination that the cause of death in case number KN01/421 was unascertained." We move up to the prior paragraphs on the summary, it notes in the injuries: "The injuries to bone, that of the right side of the face and the shoulder region, showed significant features of post-mortem antefactual injury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Artefactual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Artefactual. I apologise, Judge, "artefactual injury. There were no fresh injuries of antemortem or pari-mortem nature." Going back to the last line after -- finishing that paragraph, the next one-line paragraph: "The cause of death is unascertained anatomically." These are the UN autopsy reports, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, from 2001. That's six years after the event. Is that well-understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is well-understood. That of course showed no gunshots to the cranium as the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, not necessarily not to the head but not to the -- and that of course, is a matter to be explored, to what extent it is possible at all to shoot in the head. For example, in the neck would be -- but the witness didn't see it herself, so there are questions left. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But, ma'am, you yourself never saw these bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see those two bodies. I was standing outside the door. I didn't want to go in, but many UN staff members went in, and I'm sure that there exists photographs of those two bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ma'am, who in the UN told you that these two men had been shot in the head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall. I know that because there were so many of them. I don't know whether I was just standing there and whether I heard it or whether somebody told me that specifically. There were UN civilian police members, the press office, the UN military observers, quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, ma'am, you can't give us one name of anybody that told you this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you, I can't recall exactly who spoke to me or whether perhaps I just stood there and listened to what they were saying to each other, but I remember what they said about how those people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, staying with the UN personnel that was there, can you give us a name or names of UN personnel that were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was the entire UN military observer team there. One of them was Swiss. There was another man who was Spanish. I think that one was named Peter. There was Alun Roberts. I can't recall who was there from the UN civilian police, but there would usually be two or three of them in each team. But there is usually an official report that shows who was present of the officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Other than Alun Roberts, can you give us the name of any UNMO that was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one of them was called Peter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have a last name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I know the Swiss UNMO by the name of Peter. I can give the name. I don't want to testify, but I'm happy to pass it on to the Defence after the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if you're interested, then Mr. Waespi will tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Waespi. I'm very interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ma'am, you also in September of 2003 went to a village called Crnogorac. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The hamlet of Crnogorci. The village itself is Polaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you did speak to a woman there in that village, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that three old women remained in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I stand corrected, Judge. I believe I said in the transcript that it was September of 2003. It was 3 September 2005 -- 1995. Excuse me. I'm confused with the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you went to Crnogorac on the 3rd of September and you talked to this woman she told you about a woman by the name of Mika Crnogorac who had been killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, she also told you of the names of the people who were left in the village, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the person that she referred to as Mika Crnogorac, her actual name was Ilinka Crnogorac, but she was known as Mika, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly. I can't really remember all those names. If I wrote it down, it was fresh in my memory. It was based on the notes that I kept in those days. Now I cannot recollect all those names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ma'am, when you went there, the woman told you about a Mika Crnogorac dying, but not two women, Mika Crnogorac and Ilinka Crnogorac, did she?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lady that was killed, her surname was Crnogorac. I cannot just now remember what her first name was. It's in my statement because it is based on my notes. And another three ladies were there. They all have similar names, sometimes identical ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, we're talking about ICTY statement page 13. That's P2, which the witness refers to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's also possible to identify that piece in the witness statement and put it onto the screen so that everybody can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although if it's one or two lines then it can be read to her but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you went there it reads as follows: "On 3 September we went to Crnogorci, Mala Polaca and heard about the killing of a woman on the previous day. Her name was Mika Crnogorac, 67 years old. Five women had remained in the hamlet." Now, the woman told you about the death of a Mika Crnogorac, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: She didn't tell you about the killing of a separate woman whose name was Ilinka Crnogorac, did she?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just know of this woman that was killed who was in the house next to hers because I saw a pool of blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the name Mika Crnogorac is also used as a name for Ilinka, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if we look at the murders and the clarification schedule, and this is the clarification schedule submitted by the Prosecution, in Mala Polaca there are two killings that were listed, one for Ilinka Crnogorac on the 16th of August, 1995, and another for Mika Crnogorac on the 29th of August, 1995. But no one in that village, ma'am, ever told you that there were two women who were killed, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about this woman that was killed. I don't know about any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As you look it now, ma'am, is it clear to you that Mika Crnogorac and Ilinka Crnogorac are the same person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shouldn't we first lay a foundation for any knowledge of this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because to ask her where it's the same person where she says, she clearly testified that she received information about one person killed, what you're now more or less putting to her is that the person she talks about is the same person as another person of which she says she doesn't know anything. So I don't know whether that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll move on, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us talk about Anda Rusic. You testify about approximately August 21st going on patrol to Plavno. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you talked to a woman there by the name of Marija Jelnic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring P11 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you guide us to the relevant --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There's only one paragraph, Judge, and it's about the -- this is one of the documents that was submitted into evidence yesterday by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking you were taking her to a part of her statement, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We were talking about just generally the statement itself, Judge, is page 10 -- this is P2, by the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could interrupt. This P11 should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's admitted under seal. Therefore it will be on the screen for the witness and for us but not for the outside world. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, this is the event that we are talking about which took place on the 22nd of August, 1995, where we talk about the death of an Anda Rusic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the UNCIVPOL reporter reported that: "The death is believed to have occurred during military attack." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see another error here. It says here that it is a male and in the UNCIVPOL sometimes they did not provide sufficient details. For example, here they talk of a man but it was a woman and that was quite obvious. So there is an error there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the report does say the death took place in a military attack, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it says, but when I saw the woman she was already dead, so I don't know how she was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So given the fact that you have no idea how she was killed, you have no basis to question whether or not this statement by an UNCIVPOL commander was correct or incorrect, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very fact that it says that it was a man rather than a woman I can say that the sentence is incorrect. I remember the gentleman very well. I think he's from Nigeria. As for the rest of the sentence, I cannot comment on it. All I can say is that I saw the woman in a terrible condition. Animals had already eaten up one hand. Only the bones remained. It was one of the more horrific scenes that I witnessed there. I didn't look any more closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ma'am, let us turn our attention to yet another of the murders on the clarification schedule, Savo Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this is referred to in the P2 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sava Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I stand corrected. You're absolutely right. Sava Babic. That's referred to in the P2, Your Honours, page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, this particular incident -- this particular incident that you went to on the 4th of September, did you actually do the interviewing of the person involved in this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what interview you're talking about. If we're talking about Sava Babic, I saw her dead. I never saw her alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you follow what happened to that case after you received this information and gave it to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about the killed Sava Babic in the village of Mokro Polje in the hamlet of Babici. It was the most horrible scene I ever saw. I know that a day or two before that a patrol visited her and she complained that she had been mistreated by Croatian soldiers, that they had taken out her Fico car out of the garage, and she asked members of the civilian police to park the car once again. When we came two days later, we found the woman killed in the most horrific way anyone could be killed. She was lying -- I apologise. She was in a half-lying position in the car, in the driver's seat, with a bullet in her head, and her whole brain had fallen out on the seat next to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let me show you a -- do you need a minute, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take your time if you need, Witness 136.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The car -- the body was decomposed. Her whole brain was on the co-driver's seat. There was a Canadian lady, Jane, who took photographs of all this. She went inside and made a photograph of the whole scene. So I think you will have a clear evidence of the way in which the woman was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, ma'am, in fact the investigation charged a HV soldier with this crime, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appreciate the fact that somebody was charged with such an inhumane crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that person that was charged was a HV soldier, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was charged that he was a HV soldier. I can just assume it. I don't know who could have killed her in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ever tell the Office of the Prosecutor that you knew that somebody had been charged with this crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that anyone was charged. I don't know that anyone was charged for any one, any single crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be a matter of interpretation of the line: "I appreciate the fact that somebody was charged with such an inhumane crime." That is perhaps not a totally ambiguous line. The witness has now clarified that she doesn't know, but do I understand you well that by learning now that you appreciate that this has happened? Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Today I hear for the first time that anyone was charged for this. Maybe I used the wrong word in saying I appreciate it. I'm glad would be better perhaps that somebody was charged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we can turn our attention to ID0228 through 236.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Needs a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D9 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Waespi, will the Chamber at any later stage receive further information or evidence about what we just discussed, that is a person charged for this incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I will inquire into that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if we can go to this first page, and if we can blow that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There it comes already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is a civil police Ministry of the Interior, naturally, police report concerning the killing of a Sava Babic, the victim that the witness talked about. And if we can scroll down one, two, three, four, five -- page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems as if the document is a one-page document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It should be a multi-page document, Your Honour, that is in fact goes from 228 to 236.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The page you need is on your screen at this moment, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, as we can see this is a criminal report concerning Sava Babic, and it's drafted by an individual by the name of Mario Djukic as part of the Ministry of the Interior. And if we could go to the next page. It notes that Mario Djukic, the alleged perpetrator, is in fact a member of the 3rd Battalion of the 134th Home Guard Regiment. As we can see, this is Mario Djukic being charged with the Sava Babic incident. Now, if we may -- and, Judge, if I may, the date of the initial criminal report on this matter is 19 September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, you noted for us that in discussing P7 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I do believe that this is a document that you did not want shown publicly, P7 being a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, is it assured that P7 does not appear for the public? Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, this is a list of documents -- of individuals that you received from the civil police. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And is it not true that the civil police had provided multiple lists over time concerning the dead? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I think we received at least three lists from the Croatian civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you received those from the civilian police and not from General Gotovina. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the police station of the Croatian civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in this particular document that we have here, and I do believe there's a translation, there are listed numerous soldiers of Vojnik, as part of the dead, isn't -- aren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that there are all the men are said to be soldiers, but it doesn't mean that they were soldiers if they wore camouflage uniforms. I said that my grandfather who was 84 years old had a camouflage uniform as he had no other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, ma'am, they are listed as soldiers in this document, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you said yesterday, and this is on page 637 on line 13: "The list originated from the Croatian police and I have to say I was quite surprised at the time that we were now receiving a list of those killed."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I was allowed in the police station to make copies and to distribute them to the people in the base because they were interested in seeing who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you went --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 136, you earlier said that all the men are reported here as being soldiers. May I ask you to carefully look at a document before you give such statements, because I find at least a couple of males being reported as civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Perhaps I generalise things a little, but I see that most of them are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought you would have is to look through the whole of the list, but that's -- that's another matter how reliable the identification as soldiers or civilians is, but that's not something at this moment I think you could shed any further light on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ma'am, just to wrap this up, you just noted for us that you were permitted to make copies of these documents and to distribute these documents. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, because the people who were in the headquarters, they constantly required information about who had been killed, who had survived, and this was one of the ways that we could provide information to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly two or three questions in closed session and I'll be finished. Private session, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd just like to clarify what exhibits have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, until now I think we have had -- in fact, I'd like to invite you to consider whether D1, D2, D3, and D4 whether you have any objections because there is no formal decision yet on their admission. These were documents tendered yesterday. Then I think that D5, D6, D7, and D8 were admitted into evidence -- no, D8 not yet. Then D8 and D9 still need a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe in relation to D9 it consists of several documents. We were shown the one on 2nd January, 1996, in relation to perpetrator Mario Djukic, and I think in the same vein a document dated 19 September 1995 has been discussed. Is that the same exhibit? Is it a different document? We don't have any objections, Mr. President, because it's a fact that these documents look authentic, but of course a link to this witness is very, very tenuous. I just note that the tendering via this witness might be a problem, but we don't object for this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's a matter that came into my mind. Of course it was me myself who asked whether we would hear any further evidence on -- on a person being charged, or at least investigated, for that incident. Then the Defence came up with this document. Of course I wondered what type of questions would be put to this witness, and I wondered also whether this was a document that should necessarily be introduced through this witness or whether there could be another way of being tendered from the bar table such as not opposed by the Prosecution as a contemporaneous report reflecting that an investigation was made. I did not yet see a charge, but that's perhaps also a very technical expression whether someone is charged or suspected of or under investigation for. Therefore, if the parties could agree on whether that report on which, I think, no questions were yet put to the witness -- questions were put to her. Then the document was introduced, but I don't remember, but I would have to check whether you put any questions to this witness in relation to -- not to the event but to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I did not, Judge. She simply said she didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you put the document on the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore it's -- you are more or less tendering this from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi, I also do understand that there is no objection against that. So this witness -- this document is not introduced through this witness but is tendered from the bar table. Then, Mr. Waespi, for D1, D2, D3, D4 yesterday, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D1 through D4 are admitted into evidence. Then we come to D5, D6, D7 have been decided. D8. Any objection, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then for D9, Mr. Kehoe, let me just see. D9 was the report, isn't it? Let me just check it. Yes. That report, that was a document which consists of several pages. We have seen one more particular --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is the multiple-page document that we tendered from the bar. It is multiple pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is the whole of the document about the same investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, but I just note that at least I remember having seen two differently dated documents. Which date has the document which is D9?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The way it follows, Judge, chronologically is that first there's a criminal report and then there is a document charging this particular individual that happens thereafter in 1996. So if I may, the first document is the criminal report of 19 September 1995. Then we have another report from 2 January 1996, where Mario Djukic is charged with the -- to that detriment -- or the killing of Sava Babic. So that's why it's two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would be appreciated if there would be a hard copy of these documents for the Chamber so that we don't have to spend time on it, that we can just browse through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least one but preferably three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed. Then D8 and D9 are admitted into evidence. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have yielded the floor. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You yield the floor. Then we are in open session. For the Cermak Defence. Are you the next one, Mr. Kay, to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 136, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay, who is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The first questions I'll ask you about, Witness 136, concern your statement P00002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 1996 statement. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I give that reference in that way, Your Honour, as it's a way of linking later on electronically to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's perhaps for -- all parties are aware that if you give the full number of the -- that on the transcript it appears in blue so that it links to the e-court system, that it links to the document. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But I understood that P2 is enough to identify. It just needs to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The registrar confirms this by nodding. So a reference to P2 would do, although we do note that these are all six-digit numbers, at least in the system if you try to search for it you need the zeros, but for the link it appears sufficient to say P2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was following my training, Your Honours, from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Right. I had a similar training once, but Madam Registrar tells us that life is even more easy than we thought it already was. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the benefit of the Court, I'm looking at page 4 of the statement, and it's the fourth paragraph down beginning "In the first three days."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Witness 136, you have no need to worry about that. It's just to help the Judges and help the bar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In that passage of your statement you deal with three days that you were within the UN camp in Knin, and I'm going to ask you whether you recollect whether there was a visit by Mr. Akashi, who was a special representative of the United Nations Secretary-General.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I think it was on the 7th of August, but I did not hear Mr. Akashi's speech. I didn't listen to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you present or in his company in the camp when he visited it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. I think I had some administrative things to do in the office, and I didn't really go out to attend the meetings that he had on that day. I was not part of his entourage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware or did you see that he toured around the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that he toured the base. I know that he spoke to people. I know that he attended some official meetings outside of the base, but I myself did not see him because I had some other tasks to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I wanted to ask you about that matter. After that visit, the UN had their restriction of movement within the camp removed and members of the United Nations on the next day, the 8th of August, were able to go out into Knin and the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. The first time I went out into Knin I thought it was official. That was the 9th of August, when we went to this meeting at the police station, and a couple of days later we received permission signed by General Cermak, that we, the interpreters working for the United Nations could move about but only within the boundaries of the town of Knin itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at a document to see whether you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If the registry could call up from the Prosecution's 65 ter list number 2736.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it need a number, Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay, does it need a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It will but it will be a document that will become very familiar to the Court during the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sure it's not going to be a problem but we haven't been advised of any of the exhibits to be used by the Defence of Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We were informed by e-mail that all the Prosecution 65 ter exhibits had been uploaded into the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's a different matter from using it in cross-examination, because there might be quite a number of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore parties are under a duty to -- to the extent they know that they'll use certain documents in cross-examination to inform the -- in this case the Prosecution, at the end of the examination-in-chief about documents they're going to use so that the Prosecution can also prepare and further look at that document in preparing for further re-examination of the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, if I could just raise one matter. We believed this was already in the system but apparently it's not, and it just arises ex improviso from yesterday as the result of the witnesses's evidence concerning the pass. I do have hard copies here. I don't know whether the Bench would welcome receiving these at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have them then it we would be good that we receive them. It very much depends on the document. If it's a five-line document it might not always be necessary to provide us with a hard copy but try to imagine what our task is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It is a simple document that, as I say, you'll become familiar with during the trial. Perhaps if the usher could put one before the witness and we can see if she can identify it first, because then we won't need to go any further if that's not the case. Mr. Usher, if you could just put it in front of the witness first. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Witness 136, is this the document that you recognise as being a general pass for the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit I destroyed the pass a few years ago. I never thought that it could be used in evidence. I don't recall the words "Drnis" being there. I remember that we were allowed to move around Knin. It was a smaller pass. It was printed on paper that was thicker, and I think it allowed us to move only around the town of Knin itself. So I'm not sure this is the one. The words "main roads" were not there, and those words that if we veered off those main roads that we were doing that on our own responsibility. I don't think that it was printed on my pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've no need to go any further with this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you still want to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's no need. It will come through into the evidence in a very clear way in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it will -- I'm just wondering whether it would still keep its number, that it remains to have the status of marked for identification so that we know at least what document it was that the witness said she did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. If that assists the Court, that's something we gladly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's so we have a complete record of what happened in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. If Madam Registrar could give --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We then would have for this document number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D10 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D10 and it would keep at this moment the status of marked for identification. Please proceed. It's not tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because General Cermak issued a documents in a series of correspondence to General Forand relating to the unblocking of the UN from that camp on the 8th of August, do you recollect that as happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had any contacts with the General Forand, so I don't know anything about their correspondence, but I'm increasingly certain that the document that you showed me was not the text that we had on our passes, because our passes indicated that we were only free to move around the town of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The document that we've looked at clearly enables a person to travel in the Knin-Drnis area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Drnis. I had the pass only for Knin. But I ventured far further afield.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were working with the UN, you were able to travel outside Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was on my own responsibility, and that is why many of the interpreters did not dare to do so. I did there, but I knew that I was responsible for any consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And indeed your statement that we've looked at shows that you travelled around the region.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did travel. I went far from Knin, and I cannot now believe that I actually dared to take so many risks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The people when you travelled who you were with were -- were all from the UN camp or the European Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not European Community. I don't think that I patrolled with them at any time. There were UN military observers and a UN civilian police. I never went out on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So are you telling me that when you went out on your journeys those were not journeys that were mixed journeys between the UN and the European Monitoring Mission, European observers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were joint patrols. We called them HRAT teams, Human Rights Action Teams, that were mostly composed of the people from the press office, the UN military observers, UN civilian police, maybe even the UN military police, but as for the European Community, I would encounter them from time to time, but I did not go on patrols with them specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The first day that you left the camp was the 9th of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, to attend the meeting at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that police station was with the chief of the Knin police station; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Turn to page 5, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The first meeting was attended by the chief, Mr. Cedo Romanic, his deputy Mr. Zvonko Gambiroza and another person. I'm not quite sure, I think that this person had come from Zagreb, possibly, from some ministry or other. But I don't recall that person's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would that have been the commander of the Knin police station, Mr. Mihic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The third person was not Mr. Milos Mihic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But as it happens when you had that meeting with Mr. Romanic and the UN representatives, you presumably were acting as the translator for the UN officers speaking to Mr. Romanic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was there as an interpreter, but I have to admit that although they tried talking to Mr. Romanic, it was Mr. Gambiroza who provided all the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of the meeting between the UN representatives and the local police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that first meeting quite vividly. On the agenda of that meeting was the reopening of the UN civilian police stations in Knin itself and the area around it. In other words, the UN civilian police was supposed to resume its normal activities and start patrolling the area. Another issue that was raised was whether the UN personnel and their auxiliary staff, in other words the interpreters, may go out and retrieve their personal belongings that remained in the apartments that they were renting, and permission was given for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dealing with the first part of your answer about the opening of the UN police station, whereabouts was that in Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first police in Knin was opened near the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was there a police station opened for the local Knin police, the Croatian Knin police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that seven police stations were operational at that time and two substations of the Croatian police. I don't know how many UN police stations were operational or open. I can't recall where they were located. They were being opened -- opened gradually, and I didn't really go out into the field, and I was located at the headquarters so I can't recall where the UN police stations were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This first meeting, did that take place in the Knin police station as run by the local Croatian police commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the same building that had been used by the Serbian police before, so it was in the very same building. It was in Mr. Cedo Romanic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how far was the UN police station from this building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the UN police station was not opened outside of the headquarters or the base. The base was maybe a kilometre and a half, two or three kilometres, away on the other side of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Moving to the second part of the original question about the meeting. You referred to being given permission by the police chief Romanic to go to UN properties to collect personal belongings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Romanic, and Mr. Gambiroza because he did most of the talking, allowed for several UN teams to go out into the field, but we were supposed to supply the names of the interpreters and team members who would go out on that specific day and visit the apartments that belonged to them and to their colleagues to retrieve those personal belongings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the UN offices that you were with, did they accept the terms that were being given to them by Mr. Romanic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was accompanied by Mr. E.J. Flynn from the Human Rights office and the head of the UN civilian police Mr. Norman Boucher or something like that. They were with me, but Mr. Boucher was from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You've referred to being present over the next month at various places where crimes had been committed, and you were able to make observations when you were part of the UN team visiting such locations. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, I saw quite a few people who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you more about that. I'm just setting the ground for the next question as we've got your statement that gives the detail. Did you accompany the UN police or UN monitors who had observed crime scenes in the region? Did you accompany them to report them to the local police station in Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, they seldom went on patrols without interpreters. I was one of the interpreters who was most often prepared to go out with them, and that's exactly what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if you could just tell us what the procedure was then. Your statement clearly details you moving around the region, that you made observations. The Prosecution have introduced a few documents which are linked to occasions when you were in the area. How was the procedure adopted by which these incidents or what you had seen, how was it reported to the local police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the procedure that had been agreed was as follows: If any foreign observer team finds a dead body, first the report is to be made to the UN civilian police and then the UN civilian police informed the Croatian police either in writing or orally and then the Croatian police was supposed to notify the Croatian civilian protection and they were supposed to pick up the bodies and bury them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just looking at that procedure which you've given in a very clear way, I'd like to look at it in a little bit more detail. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's apparent from your evidence that the UN personnel you were with didn't speak the Croatian language sufficiently well to communicate to the local police commander.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So presumably you would be interpreting if you were involved in such a report between the UN personnel and interpreting to the local police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If it was done orally. If it was done in writing, it was done by my colleagues who had not agreed to leave the UN base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we just deal with -- with your role, but that's very helpful that you've told us that it was also done in writing. Did you go to the local police station in the region where you were? It may not necessarily have been Knin. It might have been another of the seven police stations. Did you go there with the team to report inside the office at the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes I'd go, because at times, specifically for the bodies that were in Zelenbabe, we made at least 10 reports asking for the bodies to be removed because the bodies had been there for 20 days at least. We went to the police station and we notified them. Sometimes we would tell about that to the police patrols if we encountered them, but I didn't go to any other Croatian police stations in the Knin area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you only report then to the Knin police station rather than any of the other district stations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if any other teams made any reports to other police stations, but I specifically made those reports only at the Knin police stations either with the duty police officer or at the Knin police station which was located at the same building where Mr. Cedo Romanic and Mr. Gambiroza were located. That was in the town centre, the centre of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Presumably you would be translating back to the UN personnel what you had been spoken about by the local police officer, be it the chief or one of the more junior officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I was the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when you were in the Knin police station, what was the set-up? Did you go to a desk where there was an officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit that we never did spend much time there when we made those reports. It was always done in passing, because we always had so many tasks and so many places to go to. So we did not sit down there and talk at length. We just said bodies were found at such-and-such a place and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was a report handed over or a list of details handed over to any of the officers, police officers, at the station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any written reports being submitted in my presence, but it is quite possible that the translators working on written reports did that, but you have to check that with the UN representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. The details that you gave to the police officer in the police station, were they recorded by that police officer in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I remember, though, that the police patrol would sometimes be with us. Actually, when we found bodies they would come fairly quickly, but I don't recall how this administrative procedure went exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the officer that you would speak to at the Knin police station, was it the same officer or was it different officers to whom these reports were made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it -- those were different police officers. I don't really remember them all. I remember maybe three or four police officers that I could recognise now, but there were many of them, so I don't remember them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many times did you visit the Knin police station to make these reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Perhaps ten times, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did they require the UN to sign for any information or sign any report that had been made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, these were -- these conversations were much too formal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just taking up the last word that you used there, was this an informal reporting procedure that you made to the police station saying to them what you had seen in relation to a body in a road or a place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I misspoke. That's how it was. We would come in. We would say that's what we saw here or there. We tried to describe the location as specifically as possible, and that's how it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Did you know if the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- police officers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I'm looking at the clock. Could you find a suitable moment for a break within the next two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'll be continuing with this subject but if I may be permitted just to finish this question, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- it follows on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know if the police officers you were speaking to were from the region or whether they were from outside the region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Do you mean whether they were from Knin originally or -- I don't understand your question in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. This is a newly liberated area. I don't know if they had local people working in the police station or people that had been drafted from outside the region to lend a hand whilst the police station was being set up. Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but you know that I myself am not from Knin originally, so I wouldn't be able to recognise any of the returnees. I didn't actually recognise any of them, and I never got into that kind of conversation with any of them in which I would be asking them where they were from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't putting it in quite that formal way but whether they'd said, "I don't know where this village is. You'll have to point it out to me because I don't know this part."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I went to most of these villages then for the first time and sometimes for the last time. So as you can see from my statement, my descriptions were very detailed. Two hundred metres from the intersection with the main road. I had to describe this in much more detailed terms because of my own ignorance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break. Before we do so, Mr. Kehoe, I had a closer look at D9 and there seems to be some ambiguity in the language as a person being charged for the event the witness described. You started using the expression "charged by the investigation," which I understand to be that the investigation points at this person as a likely perpetrator. Now, the document of the 3rd of January, 1996, I see, seems to be a report sent by the police to the military prosecutor's office just giving the result of the investigations. Now, in terms of charging people, I also see that suspect has been interviewed when he was in Zadar prison. The document doesn't -- is not clear as to why he is in Zadar prison, whether it's for this incident, for any other reason. Is there any follow-up known as far as charges against this person in the more formal sense, that is being charged before a court and then whether convicted or acquitted? Is there any follow-up? Because you tendered this from the bar table so we're not limited to what the witness told us about this, because the Chamber of course is interested in follow-up given to investigations which deal with the kinds of events the witness has described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I need to get some follow-up documentation on this. There is followup documentation I've been informed, and I will supplement this with possibly a 9A, D9A exhibit to give the complete dossier on this particular subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so we really know what the follow-up finally resulted in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what it encompassed. So then we will have a break until five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm turning to page 15 of Exhibit P2, and it's just finishing this matter of reporting to the police, Madam Witness. In your statement you detail an occasion when you visit your uncle's apartment, and you'd had a permission from Mr. Romanic to visit there, and you went with a UN officer and a local policeman; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The local policeman started stealing from your uncle's apartment, I take it under your very nose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as we entered the apartment and I gave his name, he took out a black plastic bag and started putting things inside saying he was getting married soon and that he needed these things, and he said, "I know your uncle from our school days. He's a good man. I remember him, and tell him that I'm taking this as a memento," and he filled the bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did the UN officer tell him not to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN officer was in front of the entrance. He didn't come inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you report it to the UN officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him this, but it didn't attract any attention. Everyone was taking whatever they could left and right. The flat had already been looted, so one thing more or less it didn't make much difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Romanic and report it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Last matter I'm going to ask you questions about, and I'm turning to page 10 of Exhibit P2, third paragraph down dealing with the 21st of August. Witness 136, on that day you visited the Plavno area. If you could just confirm that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't remember the exact date. I can't see the statement, but I did visit Plavno, and I can assume the incident you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can take it the date is right in your statement of 21st of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the dates in my statement are based on the notes I kept at the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it was on that day that you went with a large number of UN officers. There was the UNHCR, UNCIVPOL, UN observers, civil affairs, and in your statement it says military police. Was that UN military police or a military police from the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: UN military police. UN military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: About how many people are we talking about going into the region on that day, the 21st of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were quite a lot, because the plan was for General -- for the general allowed people from Plavno to seek shelter in the UN base, and that is why we went there. I know there were two trucks with Kenyan soldiers. There was an Indonesian ambulance and some ten or so Indonesian soldiers or medical staff. There was a UNHCR car with the main representative of that organisation. A car of the UN civil affairs with the lady who was the head of that office. And I think another two vehicles of the UN civil police. I can't tell you the number but there were many of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That gives a clear picture, if I may say so, of the numbers of people, but this was a project set up by General Forand; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our -- in the previous visit to the village of Plavno the people were afraid and they said that 11 people had already been killed in the village and they had buried them between the houses because they were frightened, and they said that they wanted to seek shelter at the UN base. I passed this on at -- to the UN base, and whether it was General Forand or someone below him that made this decision, but it was decided that we should try and transport the people who wanted to seek shelter on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, if you would allow me for one clarifying question. You described the -- those who participated in that mission on that day. Do I understand you well that this was the total of people that is -- that after you had split up that you were in a smaller group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason for us splitting up is that UN representatives, especially the civil affairs, they talked to the people. Some people had already come with their small bundles, and they said it would be best for them to stay there for a few more days to register with the Croatian authorities, that they would make sure that they would be safe in the village, and they tried to postpone their transfer to the UN compound. After that, we split into two groups and decided to carry out a more detailed patrol of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then you were in a smaller group after you had split up. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were any of the people in the district that you were concerned with on this day actually taken back to the UN camp, transported, if you like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A man from the village of Otrici who said that he had been wandering in the woods for about 15 days and hiding there, and another man who said that he was on the verge of a nervous breakdown and that he couldn't wait for another day for that registration. So these two men did go back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's about the registration that I'm going to ask you some questions now. That was registration with which authority?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were told that UN staff would talk to the Croatian authorities for these people who remained to be registered, I assume with the Croatian police, to be received some ID documents. That was the promise they was given -- the promise they were given, that they would be registered with the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it seems although the group from the UN went there on that day, the actual mission of taking the people to the UN camp was not achieved.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have to admit that the whole situation disturbed me, because I saw how terrified the people were. I saw that the so-called cleansing of the village had started, Zaturc [phoen] and Torbice, to the left of Plavno, and I realised that the real cleansing was only beginning, and I expected other incidents, and I was sorry and, unfortunately, there were other incidents. The incident in Grubori I occurred just a couple of days later and I am really sorry that the people who had been ready to move had they had been taken to the UN camp, the incident in Grubori would have been avoided. I was seriously disturbed when I realised that they would be left there without protection and I didn't wish to interpret. It was my colleague who took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So General Forand's plan for that day was not followed through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
