utterances.text: No, it wasn't, because it was quite easy to persuade old people not to leave their homes, that they should keep their homes, that they would be protected, and they gave them some hope that they could stay where they were, because nobody really wanted to abandon their homes. They were elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The purpose was to register them as individuals in the area with the police. That was the purpose, was it, that caused them to be left there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The representative of civil affairs explained to them that they would contact the Croatian authorities, the Croatian police, and as a result they would be given protection, and the number of people remaining would be registered, and through this registration they would be given protection, and they would receive ID documents, and that was what was promised to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. It seemed a long way, but it was about that matter that I was asking you -- you questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that finishes my questioning of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Mikulicic. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic, who is counsel for Mr. Martic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Witness 136. As His Honour has said, my name is Goran Mikulicic, and I am an attorney, Defence counsel for the third accused General Markac. Allow me to put a few questions to you. Without wasting time, let me ask you a few questions that you can simply answer with a yes or no. Is it true that you were employed as an interpreter for the civilian police of the United Nations from the 11th of June, 1994 until the 16th of September, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From the month of August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true that in your statement you declared that you were of Serbian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that finding employment in the UN, you signed a kind of contract and a statement of some kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us in a few sentences what kind of statement you signed when finding employment with the UN?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contract itself implied that we must not reveal any information, that we must observe everything and respect everything that was going on at the UN. It meant observance of all the rules of the United Nations, including the confidentiality of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that include your obligation to be impartial in relation to the environment you're working in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. My work was of a humanitarian nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. We'll move on to your work. You were an interpreter, were you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What were the duties of an interpreter in the UN civil police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period when I worked in Vrlika, I occasionally interpreted orally meetings with the police, but I worked for the longest period of time in Vrlika, but the rest was patrolling the area and visiting the remaining Croatian inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand that. But when you say patrolling, does that include -- does that imply that you personally were investigating something or were you accompanying people who were doing the investigation as an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an interpreter, and we visited the Croats who were there, mostly elderly people. Whether everything was all right, whether they had enough food, whether anyone was mistreating them. Sometimes I would buy them things out of my own pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand that. In your statement, in several places you said that you prepared certain lists. Let me remind you. You visited the Knin cemetery and you made a list which has been produced as evidence in this case. Were you doing that as part of your duties as an interpreter of the UN civil police or did you do that upon your own initiative?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Working at the UN camp I would repeatedly come across questions from people as to who had been buried at the Knin cemetery. So with the approval of my superior I made such a list for an official report and also for my personal notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand that, madam, but my question was whether this was an instruction given from one of your superiors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I also said --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many interpreters were employed at the Knin camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many before the Storm, but 15 of us remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many interpreters were employed in the UN civil police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many before the Storm, but four of us remained from the civil police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am referring to your statement, so please correct me if I'm wrong. One of the four interpreters was of Croatian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before the reference line 52, 16 to 18 disappears, the question was whether drawing up that list was done on the instructions given from one of your superiors, the witness said: "No, but I also said" and then it stops. If the witness could repeat what her explanation was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you, Witness 136, could you please repeat your answer that you gave to your -- your rather short answer you gave to the question whether it was -- whether you were instructed to make this list. The answer was no, but then you added something. Could you please repeat what you then added.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I didn't receive any instruction, but it was appreciated if I provided any additional information to the UN civil police about the remaining people. If I took note of that, either about the people who remained or about the people who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we then have to understand your answer as it's written that they thanked you for this additional activity?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was counsel who said thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's now -- I see that there is some confusion about who said what. I think that my question lacks further relevance and that the matter is clear enough unless -- Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- this might be an opportune time just to mention that when counsel and the witness are speaking in the same language that they're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was considering to tell this in advance, but Witness 136, you are speaking the same language as Mr. Mikulicic. Therefore, often you start answering the question already when the translation of the question has not yet been finished. So could you make a short break. And, Mr. Mikulicic, would you make a short break before you put your next question to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So from what we've heard, by making those lists and notifying the people about their close relatives who may have been killed or not, this is what you did on your own initiative because you wanted to assist people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could I please refer you to a paragraph in your statement beginning with the word "among." You said that there was a Croat woman by the name of (redacted). She was employed as an interpreter there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mikulicic, finding a paragraph starting with "Among" where we have some 15 pages causes some problems. Could you tell us which statement, the 1996 or the later statement, and then also where approximately to find it. I have only the -- it's only in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I see a reference on page 4, on Exhibit page 2, the second complete paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you referring to the paragraph which starts with "Among us interpreters was a Croat woman"? Is that the paragraph you're drawing the attention of the witness to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That's the paragraph that I'm referring to. Unfortunately, the transcript does not reflect my words what I said, that it was a paragraph at page 4. What I omitted to say is that I'm talking about the 1996 statement. So I do apologise. I hope I won't be making any more references of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So let us go back to the question, Witness 136. Is it true that among you interpreters there was a Croat woman by the name of (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident, if I may call it that, when you made a protest about her conduct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: According to your statement, she conveyed the information to the Croat soldiers outside of the UN base; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Two paragraphs further down in your statement you say that there were quite a few Croats inside the UN camp. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, my question to you is as follows: What was the motive? What led you to protest against the fact that your colleague notified the Croat soldiers outside of the camp about Croats inside the camp where in fact you did the same thing for some other persons of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, this is a composite question, the first part of the question being what moved this witness to do what she did. Then you intertwined with that question another matter, which is whether it was fair to do so because, as you say, she had done the same. Could you -- the second one asks for a judgement. I would not oppose against asking such a question whether she considered herself that to be fair, but could we split up those questions clearly? So the first thing, Witness 136, Mr. Mikulicic would like to know is why you complained about the behaviour of (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can we briefly go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 136, could you tell us why you complained about, but -- but before you do so. Mr. Mikulicic, in your question it was implied that -- at least let me check that carefully. Yes. You implied in your question that what the colleague interpreter did is to inform the Croats about the presence of Croats inside the camp. Now, what her statement tells us is that she told, as far as I see, she started telling them everything that was going on in the camp. That might well have included what you just mentioned, but that's not to be taken from that statement at this moment. So we'd first like to know whether this interpreter, your colleague, informed the Croat soldiers outside about the presence of Croats inside the camp. Was that part of what she conveyed to the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Her motive was of a completely different kind, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. I'm not talking about her motive at this moment, just about the content of what she told the Croatian soldiers, that is, did that cover also the presence of Croats inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What she said as she rushed out of the gate, she said, "There are over 500 people here. They are in the cinema. I am a Croat." That's all I heard her say. I didn't hear what she went on to say, because I started making protests, and the monitors who were standing there were also making protests, and her boyfriend the police sector chief was quiet, and that really upset me. I thought that he should use his official position to prevent those civilians from going out and saying things. We prevented people from going out. We shut them up in the cinema hall. I personally locked all the doors because we didn't want the drunken soldiers who would come in to know that there were civilians in the base at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mikulicic, next question I take it, still is, Mr. Mikulicic, why you complained although, Mr. Mikulicic, the last answer gives already a lot of explanation. If you'd like to put additional questions in respect to this to the witness, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think that this actually exhausted my interest in this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned the boyfriend of this interpreter that you complained about, if you allow me I will ask two more questions about your former boyfriend. We heard that he had been a member of the special forces in the army of Republic of Serb Krajina. Do you know who was the commander of this special unit of the special forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you or jog your memory. Does the name Dragan Vasiljkovic, nicknamed Captain Dragan, does it mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard of that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that the UN forces had armoured personnel carriers and other vehicles in the base where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: UN personnel did have some kind of armoured personnel carriers and also some other vehicles, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Although it is a notorious fact but just for the record, could you please tell us what colour were those vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: White.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did they bear any insignia at the sides?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "UN."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May I then conclude on your behalf, and please correct me if I'm wrong, that it was possible to recognise those vehicles very easily, even at a distance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your statement, that is the 1996 statement at page 3, the last paragraph, you say that you saw as you ran along the fence some 20 soldiers and a tank were coming on the road from Drnis, and you thought that they were "our soldiers." These are your words.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you used the word "our soldiers," were you referring to the UN soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I meant Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you referring to the army of Republika Srpska under the command of Milan Martic, who was sentenced to 35 years in prison for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the Serb soldiers that had given me protection, regardless of under whose command they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, could you please remain in unnecessary comment in your question. If you would have to refer to the sentence persons received whenever you refer to them, then it might take us some time now and then. That's one. And apart from that, it's not relevant for the question, since we all know who Milan Martic is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your statement from 1996, at page 15, the penultimate paragraph, you say that you didn't pay much attention to the Croatian soldiers and that you did not notice their unit names or the badges they wore on their uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Were you able, on the basis of the colour of their uniforms, to distinguish the Croatian army and the Croatian police units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were two kinds of uniforms, plain green and camouflage uniforms, but I don't know which were the regular army units in some and which were special units and I know that some wore ribbons on their shoulders and around their head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This brings me to the incident in Grubori which you mention in your 1996 statement at page 11. That's the 7th paragraph where you say that you were in the village of Grubori on the 26th of August; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's correct that I went to Grubori, but it was one day after the incident, not on the day when the incident took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that were accompanying UN personnel. I don't want to now list them, but that you were not allowed to enter the village. You were stopped by Croatian soldiers or the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were stopped at the check-point at the entrance to the village. We were not allowed to enter the village because they were in the process of removing the bodies from the village of Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you perhaps recollect with greater accuracy today who it was that prevented you, the UN delegation, from entering the village? Was it the police, the civilian police, the military police, or was it the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot recall even the colour of their uniforms, whether this was the police or the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have just answered the next question that I had in mind so I will not ask it. In your statement we heard that today you said that you had participated together with the civilian police of the United Nations in reporting the crimes to the police organs of the civilian authorities of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you present at any time when a crime or a complaint was reported to anyone else apart from the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only place that I went to was the civilian police station, and once to the headquarters to a meeting with the liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Although it is quite clear from your answer, let me ask you to make this absolutely clear. Were you ever a member of a team or a group that reported certain crimes or criminal activities to the units of the Special Police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the units of the Special Police were. I attended just one meeting at the headquarters. Whether the representatives there were those of the Special Police, the ordinary police or the army, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness 136, you said a little while ago that you know that members of the Special Police wore green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't know that. I said that I knew that there were two kinds of uniforms, but I don't know what kind was worn by the army and what kind by the Special Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you for your answer. Witness 136, why did you say -- now I'm talking about your 2007 statement, page 5. At the very end of this statement you said that you do not agree to your statement being used by the authorities other than the present Tribunal at the discretion of the Office of the Prosecutor of the -- this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I gave my statement to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, and before that I had also given a statement to a non-governmental organisation in Belgrade. I do not want to give any statements to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness 136, I'm not asking you whether you want or whether you don't want to give any statements to anyone else. I'm asking you why you don't want your statement that you had already given to anybody else, for anyone else's use apart from this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who else might use my statement, might want to use my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the judicial organs of the Republic of Croatia, the Republic of Serbia, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only place where I want to give my evidence right now is this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions. Thank you, Witness 136, for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Waespi, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday in answering questions from my colleague Mr. Kehoe, you talked about the time where you -- when you were working in the Vrlika area. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give us a page then we are better able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's on page 50, line 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you also, otherwise, give us a little portion of the text because the newly uploaded transcript of yesterday is with new page numbers. That's the sequential page numbering. So that starts at 616 at the moment. And you said it was page --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 50. The witness talks about Cetina being shelled before Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you just -- you said it was page 50. So 616 plus 50 makes 666. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When you said, Witness, that Cetina had been shelled several times before Operation Storm, can you first tell us where Cetina is in relation to Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cetina is a village in the area of Vrlika, very close to the separation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And is that east or west of Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't tell you that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. And when you said it had been shelled several times before Operation Storm, what time frame are you talking about? Which months and which year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It may have been a month prior to this, and it wasn't just Cetina that was shelled but the area towards Otisic and the lake there, several times, because I belonged to the harvest team which was designed to encourage people, regardless of the shelling, to go and harvest the wheat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And as far as you can recall, were there any military targets in Cetina and the other villages you say were shelled?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object, Judge. This witness has got no basis to say what is a military target and not a military target in Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think the witness can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just re-read the question. Well, we could ask perhaps not about military targets but, Mr. Waespi, perhaps you could ask the witness then whether she was aware of any military presence, military facilities such as barracks that are matters of fact that the witness could testify about. If she doesn't know, that does not necessarily mean that there were no military targets, but they could be unknown to the witness. But that is a factual question Mr. Waespi can put to the witness. So to partly your objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may just talk, one last issue here, Judge. This was not part of either direct or cross-examination, the shelling of Cetina that took place. I didn't ask any questions and I don't believe my colleagues did and certainly counsel is opening up another area. This is not redirect, it's in fact new direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, could you tell us what caused you to put this question now and not at any earlier stage seeking further clarification of the testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The way I understood redirect, Mr. President, is any issues that arise out of cross-examination. This is an issue that has been raised by Mr. Kehoe and the witness answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not ask any shelling questions about Cetina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Waespi, could you refer to the exact source where Mr. Kehoe is, as you say, dealing with this matter in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's the page reference I gave to you a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- yes. That's -- which I'm still -- let me just -- I said -- I was calculating, wasn't it. To 666 I came, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The issue was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give the literal text then it's easier to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The answer of the witness starts: "There are many elements why there was this build-up of fear in Knin. I worked in the Vrlika area and when all the nine UN stations were shut down," and then it goes on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has anyone found it already? I have not found it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And as I indicated, the issue the Defence was dealing with was that build-up of fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'll allow to put these questions. Build-up of fear. It could make a difference on whether shelling was of one type or another. Please proceed but don't ask about military targets but ask about her knowledge of military presence or military installations. Well, phrase your question as long as it does not require a judgement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, as far as you recall, as far as you remember, was there any military presence, any soldiers, any installations you were aware of at that time in Cetina or any of the other villages you mentioned having been shelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically in the village of Cetina, I think that there was absolutely no military presence, and I can say the same for the surroundings of the Peruca Lake. There was no military presence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you want to say that you were not aware of any military presence, which of course is not exactly the same as that there was no military presence, but you didn't observe anything of that kind. Is that well-understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is well-understood. I didn't notice. There may have been up in the hills somewhere, but I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to make matters clear, who was shelling these villages, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean the answer is pure speculation. I mean, she doesn't know. If she knows, was she with HV troops when the shelling was actually takes place or with ARSK troops?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, it's a quite simple question and I really have carefully listened to your colleague. The question is who did it, if you know. There are a few possible answers. One, I don't know. Then the question is answered. And if the witness says she does know, then she can tell us what she knows, and then of course we'll carefully look at whether it's knowledge of fact she observed herself or whether it was hearsay. Please answer the question. Do you know who shelled this location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went deep within the lines and I know where the observation posts of the Croatian soldiers were, and it was visible that they had approached the hill above Cetina and they were shelling from the hills above Cetina. They held their positions there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, perhaps we could further explore what exactly then the witness saw when she said that they were shelling the -- whether she did see any armament or whether she saw any crews. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, could you answer the questions the Presiding Judge is interested in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer the question. I had the good fortune that whenever I patrolled in a car with a Portuguese member of my team there was no shelling, but through UN reports you can verify that the fields where people were harvesting were shelled. And on one occasion I attended a funeral where people were terrified, because a couple of days prior to that a shell had fallen close to the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks for the answer, Witness, but the issue was whether -- what kind of armament, if you saw any armament, on the side of the Croatian army you have seen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't that close to the positions to be able to see the kind of weapon used. Even if I had been able to see it, I have no understanding of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Let me move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question there. You said you were aware of Croat positions. Were you aware of any positions of any other army in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On a number of occasions I went very deep within the lines, the villages of Koljani and Lapac to the Kenyan observation post and they showed me at a distance of perhaps a thousand metres that I mustn't show my face because there were snipers there or positions of the Croatian army. This was at a distance of some 1.000 metres from the position of the Kenyan observation post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I wasn't -- I wasn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see I haven't answered the question. No, I didn't go to the other side, so I didn't see any other observation posts or Serb-held positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I understand your answer to be that they were there, but you never went there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see Serb positions. Or maybe I didn't go far enough to reach those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Moving to the second issue. This is again yesterday's transcript, page 76, lines 19 to 24, and I read the answer of the witness to the issue of whether Knin suffered great damage. The witness said: "Well, to tell you the truth, you are running and the shells are falling all around you. You don't have an opportunity to notice many things. I saw the destroyed house, the damage to the outpatient clinic, and I saw house." In relation to this damaged house or destroyed house, do you remember prior to the start of Operation Storm whether there was any military presence in or around of that house, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was a civilian house, because that is where I waited for the UN civil police patrol to come and pick me up every morning. So it was a civilian house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. The third issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, for the record, for those who later have to look at this, if anyone, that's page 692 to 693 you just referred to. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The third issue is the issue about your boyfriend's apartment, and this is page 85 on lines 17 to 20. And you have been asked the same question a couple of times, so I just want to make sure that we know your answer. On that page 84, Mr. Kehoe asked you: "Well, did you see other soldiers living in that apartment complex?" And your answer was: "I don't know what you mean by 'soldiers.' Most of the men were in uniforms." Now, my question is: Do you know whether there were soldiers living in the house -- apartment complex your boyfriend was living in at the time the Operation Storm was unfolding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly there may have been soldiers as well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Moving on to the fourth area, just a clarification. You said on page 95, lines 16 to 17, when you were put questions about Veritas and your work in Belgrade, that you were working for the Humanitarian Law Centre. Can you just explain in one or two sentences what the Humanitarian Law Centre was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those days I was investigating crimes that occurred during the Operation Storm. So we were looking for witnesses from the Sector South and Sector North. My task was to interview the witness, take a statement, and later, in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, we tried to establish where violations were made of the human rights law, and these statements were sent directly to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And just one or two words about the institution itself, Humanitarian Law Centre. Who was the founder of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a non-governmental organisation which is still operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, the second to last issue is (redacted). You were asked about her and you gave answers, page 99, line 8 to 15. You were asked by my colleague Mr. Kehoe, and the quote is: "Well, the Croatian soldiers escorted some people who were not wounded to the UN compound, didn't they?" And you give your answer: "All I remember about that specific case was her arrival." You go on. Now, in relation to (redacted), did she come on her own to the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you just quoted a portion of the evidence which was redacted yesterday. At least that's what Madam Registrar tells me. Of course it does appear on our transcript, but -- so therefore I'm asking for a new redaction now, Madam Registrar, and could you then refrain from referring to that name. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall whether that person was accompanied to the UN compound by the Croatian soldiers or whether she came on her own, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And the last issue I wanted to discuss is P11, which is an exhibit under seal. If it could be put on the screen but not broadcasted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be on our screen. I see on the transcript I said "our screen" but I was perhaps not very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you a couple of questions about this document. It says, and I quote: "The death is believed to have occurred during military attack." Since you were the interpreter at that time, do you recall what was actually said and by whom it was said in explaining that situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that as there was smoke in the village, that is what brought us to the village. We were looking around the village, and I think it was one of the Indonesian soldiers who cried out that he had found something. We came there. The body was covered with a blanket and there was stones around it. People were hesitant to lift the blanket. When finally the blanket was removed we saw this horrific scene. No one approached close enough to establish the cause of death, because the scene was dreadful. Half of the body had been eaten up by animals. I don't know what happened later on. I assume that the Croatian police was informed about this. The body was not regularly buried, but two elderly men from a neighbouring village took the body and threw it into a septic tank which her son had dug. They were very old. They couldn't carry her. They covered the body with earth. And the next time I came, a part of the skirt of that woman was there. So she wasn't buried in the cemetery, and I don't know what the wounds were, how they were inflicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Just going back to my original question about the quote in this report saying the death is believed to have occurred during military attack. Do you remember whose explanation, whose comment, whose information that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was something that was not discussed in my presence, but I do remember this Nigerian officer but they didn't discuss it in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just a last question in clarification in regard to the apartment complex of the boyfriend.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Apart from the boyfriend, who else was living in that complex as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a large complex with many buildings. I didn't know anyone from those buildings because I didn't live in that part of the area, and I am not from Knin. So this was a housing settlement, and I don't know the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were any women and children living in there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: There is one small matter in relation to Exhibit marked for identification 10 from Mr. Kay's examination. That's the exhibit we only had a hard copy. Apparently, there is a copy in e-court which is 65 ter number 00866, which is identical to 02736. So that's a duplicate. This is marked for identification D10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now what is uploaded in e-court is unknown to this Court, because only if it is presented then we have no access to all your lists of uploaded systems. Also, I was informed by Madam Registrar just before we came to this courtroom that there was something about this numbering, especially in relation to D10. I don't know whether this is the issue. Madam Registrar could you please inform us about what you found and what you told me earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. What Mr. Waespi has mentioned is the situation in e-court so D10 marked for identification is 65 ter 866.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that resolve your problem? Then is there any further need before I invite my colleagues to put further questions? Is there any need for further cross-examination? Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just briefly on this Cetina issue in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the practice is in this Trial Chamber. In the Dragomir Milosevic case there was no re-cross after redirect, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course the re-cross is meant to deal with matters which were developed in redirect. Therefore, it's not just a new round of questioning and the second cross-examination should focus on the questions you have just put to the witness and not challenge the answers that were given in the examination-in-chief. So that -- these are the limits, Mr. Kehoe. But from what Mr. Kehoe said, I noticed that it was specifically one of the issues you further developed in re-examination that he would like to address. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll slowly learn with each other what our -- what our practice will be. It depends on how you're dealing with matters and then the Chamber will see whether it's an efficient and useful way of using our time in this courtroom. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Madam Witness, do you know if the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina had artillery positions in Cetina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Any of the other counsel? I don't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you, Witness. I'd first like to take you to your 1996 statement for the parties, page 5, where you are referring to two sisters from Uzdolje who came on Sunday, the 6th, to the UN compound. At the end of what your statement gives in this respect you say that a soldier took one person, drove her back to the place on the Knin-Drnis road near Uzdolje where they had been picked up, and then it reads: "On the arrival, she saw that the four old women had been killed. The elderly man was still alive, as he raised his head." Did you receive any information on how these four elderly women had been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interpreted their statement at the UN base upon their arrival, and the details that I remembered are what they conveyed to the UN civilian police members. They were too afraid to give their names. I don't recall them saying how the women had been killed. I remember that they said that the man had already -- had still been alive but she had not been allowed to approach him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you have no further details as to how the killing took place. Thank you. Then --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would like to take you to your statement you gave in 2007. For the parties, paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the statements. I don't see them on the screen, either of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll inform you exactly on what I'll put questions about. You stated, and I read this full paragraph of three lines: "During the month of August, I would see many soldiers from various units in the area, and I formed the impression that the military was still in control because there were so many of them still around." Could you give us further details which would allow us better to understand whether these were soldiers on duty or not? If I see a soldier in the supermarket, that's different from when I see a soldier in a military jeep. Could you give us further details which could give us a clue as to what -- whether they were on duty when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the villages that I patrolled, there would be check-points set up. I remember the check-point in the village of Otisic. We were stopped and they asked us to explain what we were doing there and why patrols were sent to this village, who we were looking for. So I would see a lot of soldiers in the villages. Primarily I saw them looting the houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course we couldn't say that when looting the houses they could have been -- well, they could have been on duty but not observe what they had to do. Could you tell us if you say -- first of all, I'd like to -- you gave one example of a check-point. Was this common in the villages, and could you give us an impression of, in total, how many of these check-points manned by soldiers you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the check-point leading towards the village of Strmica. We were not allowed to pass. I remember the check-point at the village of Plavno where we were also not allowed to pass. I think that -- I think that this gives you a picture of the fact that the Croatian army was still there on the ground in all the villages. I'd see them all over the place. And I have to admit that meeting Croatian soldiers was a much more harrowing experience for me than meeting Croatian police officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you also try to answer the other question I put to you, is that how many of those check-points in total you may have seen? Are you talking about five villages in which you saw such check-points, including hamlets, or 20 or a hundred? Could you give us an impression?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't now recall exactly, but whenever I went I remember that I went to the relay station in the direction of Drnis, and there were a hundred of them. I know that because they threatened me, and I barely got out of that situation. I remember in the village of Zelenbabe, I remember there was a lot of troops there too. In fact, I don't recall ever having entered a village and not seeing the troops there. I remember the first day when I went to my colleague's apartment to pick up her stuff. That's an area in the town centre. There was a sign saying no access and I saw Croatian troops there. I remember seeing a lot of them in my relative's village when I went there looking for my grandmother in the village of Palanka. So I saw them all over the place. I can't really tell you how many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you say "troops," are you referring to individuals in uniforms or are you talking about groups apparently with some kind of an organisation? What do you mean by troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see individual troop -- individual soldiers. They were always in a larger group of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Then I would like to take you to your 1996 statement, page 10 for the parties, where you stated about a very old woman born in 1913 who appeared with her hands up, and we are talking about your visit to the Plavno hamlets, who said, "Don't kill me. Take whatever you want." And then you were asked about a body you'd seen. She told you that her husband had left for Belgrade a week before the attack, that they had an apartment there, and she showed papers. You found another three very old women. What happened then further? You describe what you saw, what this woman told you. Did you receive any further information there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of the women said that her son, Stevan Vidovic, had gone missing a couple of days ago. That's what she complained. She didn't know what had happened. But we told her that we would definitely try to find out what had happened to her son. And perhaps some three days after that we found the body of Stevan Vidovic. I was with a security officer and another man, I think he was Canadian, in a car. The window was open, and we could smell the bodies, the decomposing bodies, and we found Stevan Vidovic's body. It was in a very advanced stage of decomposition. That was in the village of Plavno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did you see anything that would, although you not being a professional, give you any impression on how Stevan Vidovic would have died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He was on his back on the ground. He was wearing civilian clothes and his face was completely maggot-ridden, so I didn't really look to see how he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I have no further questions. If any of the parties have any questions which were caused by the matters I raised in my questions, then you have an opportunity to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Madam Witness, Judge Orie read from your 2007 statement, paragraph 15 concerning the military still in control of the area and you noted the check-points that had soldiers. Do you know if these check-points were manned by members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were soldiers, and I really don't know whether they -- whether the members of the military police have any different kind of uniforms, but the only thing that I saw them as was as soldiers at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So, Madam Witness, you cannot tell us whether or not the individuals at that check-point were regular soldiers or members of the military police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that they were soldiers, because I find it -- I would find it quite incredible that there were so many military police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, in paragraph 10 of your statement of the -- this is P3, this is the 2007 statement, you note in the last sentence: "As far as I remember, it was military people who were manning the check-points, although I could not be sure if the uniform, which was mainly camouflage, was military -- was military police."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I keep saying all the time that I did not pay that much attention to uniforms. I know that when I would come across a Croatian police officer, and despite the fact that I was involved in several incidents with them, that I felt much more comfortable than when I would encounter a Croatian soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I understand, but once again, and this is my last question, when you saw them you couldn't tell if they were soldiers or members of the military police, could you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think the witness answered two or three times already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's my last question, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kehoe, if the last question is put for the third time to a witness then it's still -- whether it's the last or the semi-last or the first -- no, first couldn't be but the third or the fourth, that doesn't make any difference. Let's try to understand what the witness wants to tell us. Do I understand, Witness 136, that on the basis of the uniforms you have seen that you say, "I could not tell you whether the uniforms I usually saw as the military uniforms, whether military police may have been dressed in such uniforms as well"? Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The only way how I could distinguish the military from the police is that I knew that the police had blue uniforms and the army had plain green or camouflage uniforms. And if this is what I said in my statement, that it was camouflage or some other kind of uniform, after so many years I can no longer have this picture in my mind's eye who stopped me at what check-point. What is written in the statement is accurate because it's based on my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it's also your testimony, if I well-understood you, that you would be surprised if the uniforms you described or you perceived as being military uniforms would be of the military police because then the number of policemen would be extremely high, if I well-understood you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you understand me well. Because as far as I know based on the structure in the UN, I know that the number of military police cannot compare to the number of soldiers, troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, any need to put a question which has not yet been answered by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the blue uniforms were the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked in the beginning and I promised you, Witness 136, that I would give you an opportunity to give details on a matter I'm not aware of but where you thought it would be good for us to know these details. You have an opportunity to do so. And if you would please start telling us what it is about that you want to give us further details so that we can find in your statements what you will give further details on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, about the body of the woman found in the village of Ivanici or Sovilji. Nobody asked me about that yesterday, and in my statement the description is a little bit more detailed than the one in the UN report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say we find further details on that in your statement compared to the UN report which gives less details. Thank you for drawing our attention to that. Shall we find that on paper already?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Regarding the injuries that led to this woman's death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, if you could help me, because I am trying to fully understand. If you give us one second to find it. Anyone who could help me is invited to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The first reference I found is in paragraph 24 of the second statement, 2007 statement, which is P3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that refers usually to the earlier statement as well. Do we find anything about it in the first statement, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps because Ivanici is near Gracac it might refer to page 9 of P2, when the witness visited on the 19th of August with Alun Roberts and other personnel, areas near Gracac where she found the woman who is 70 years old. In the other exhibit she was described as 60 years old. That's as close as I can get to this Ivanici incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me -- Witness, we find one reference to an event in Ivanici just where you say the report made is accurate, and Mr. Waespi now suggests that that is about what you had seen on the 19th of August in Sovilji. Is that the same event, same incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I can clarify and tell you what I meant. Yesterday, we mentioned an old lady, 60 or 70 years old. That's irrelevant. She was an old woman lying face down next to the creek, and a paper was going around this courtroom, nobody asked me anything, where it is specified that she had a leg injury. And I thought this was some kind of disrespect. People were saying how could she have died of her leg injury. But I also wanted to point out to you that she also had a gunshot wound to the back of her head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is -- you're now talking -- talking about a lady where you said about a woman, an old woman about 70 years, a corpse in a state of decomposition, killed by a bullet in the back of her head which you found close to a stream. Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say that if there's any other report which says that she has injuries to her leg that you'd like to emphasise that, whether true or not, but that you found this person, and if it's the same person, with a shot injury in her head.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The report that was shown here yesterday made mention of only the leg injury. It is also a fact that she also had a wound to her head and also the leg wound. But I suppose that the head injury was fatal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I don't remember exactly whether it was one of the P exhibits. I take it if it was shown. Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think that was the one which had the village of Ivanici redacted so that was -- or made illegible. Yes. It's ter number 7092.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have the P number that would certainly help had us because we don't have access to your numbers. It's P10 from what Madam Registrar tells us. I have problems there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's P10, an exhibit which can be shown openly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I see from that report that's also about an old lady. It reads: "60 years of age, dead body decomposed beside a small stream in that village." And that is the village just mentioned. So at first sight, it seems that this is the same incident although that might need clarification and the witness draws our attention to the fact that what she observed was not just leg injuries but wounds in the head. Now, you also told us that the body was decomposed. Was it not -- was the decomposition not at such a level that you could not see anymore what were wounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was not so badly decomposed. Well, there was this stench, but I wouldn't say that she was so badly decomposed, but I think that there were quite a few witnesses. So I would like you to do something to check that. She did have the hand -- the head injury in addition to the leg injury. And I hope, I think that the body was also photographed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other matter that you would like to bring to our attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Another document that was shown by Mr. Kehoe yesterday about the way in which the UN interpreters were employed. I think that's Article 18. I have to say that I was quite friendly and quite close with some of my colleagues, with many of my colleagues, and I never heard about anyone being employed by the Serb authorities. And the next article, which was not read out here, specifies that we would - the local staff would get our salaries in the local currency. That's not true either. We were not paid in local currency. We were all paid in US dollars. This is what makes me believe that this document is not credible. I hope that you will take steps to investigate the origin of this document further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think it is not up to you to give us advice on these matters and whether the conclusion should be that the document is not credible or that the rules were not observed or that, for one reason or another, this document would not apply or whether it was not replaced by another document for later stages that's still to be seen, but at least you draw our attention to the fact that you never heard that any of your colleagues was employed through this agency, if I understand you well, and that you were paid in US dollars and not in local currency. That is factual information. Mr. Kehoe, I'm looking at the clock because I thought whether we could finish with the witness before the second break which would have to have started already ten minutes ago at least. How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just briefly, Judge, I have a couple of questions concerning --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are further questions to be put to the question in relation to that which of course the witness brings new elements to our attention, then we should do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 136, where I had some hope that we could finish before the break it will be just after the break. We will have a break and we'll resume at ten minutes past 2.00, and Mr. Kehoe, how much time would you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 10 minutes, or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any of the other counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ten minutes past 1.00, I assume you mean, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We can't resume at a time that has elapsed already. Thank you for correcting me. We resume at ten minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Madam Registrar, if we could put P10 back up on the screen. I apologise, Judge. P10 I believe is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any problem with P10?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm fine. It's fine. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, I put P10 back up on the screen, and this is the document that you take issue with; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, if you recall, you do recall as in P3 that you were interviewed less than a year ago by the Office of the Prosecutor. Were you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And during the course of that interview they showed you a series of UN reports, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you had the opportunity to review those reports, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this was one of the reports that was given to you to read, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if I can direct your attention to your statement of the 11th June 2007, P3 statement, paragraph 24, you note in relation to the UNCIVPOL report with the number - and the ERN number matches, Judge - relating to the finding a body in the village of Ivanici. "I can confirm that this report accurately reflects what I was told and what I witnessed when I was working with that particular CIVPOL team." Did you say that at that time in June of 2007?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I said that, but obviously I missed to notice this detail which I did state in my statement from 2006 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you had the opportunity -- the Office of the Prosecutor gave you the opportunity to review this report and make any elaborations or additions as you saw fit, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. But on that day I was shown a large number of documents, and it is quite possible that something like this relating to the wounds evaded me. But I assure you that she had a wound to her head, and my memory was still fresh when I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: There is nothing in this UN report about a wound to the head, is there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, but I'd like you to look for other UN staff members and to see their reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And there is nothing in your statement in June of 2007 about any wounds to the head, is there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-136 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is in the statement from 1996, when my memory was much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, the fact of the matter is that none of that information is in your statement in 1996 either, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think the witness gave the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I mean, if Mr. Waespi can find it for us in this 1996 statement about these gunshot wounds to the head for this woman, I will gladly review that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, again I think there's the issue of whether it is the same event or -- yes? Could you guide us back to the page again?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, it's page 9, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second paragraph. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it clearly says, quote from the fourth line in that second paragraph: "The woman was killed by a bullet in the back of her head." That's -- I think one of the connecting features is the creek and the stream, the creek appearing in Exhibit P10 and the stream in Exhibit P2. The witness gave her explanation, and it's up to Your Honours to assess that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Date and place, whether it's the same or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you can look at it, Judge, and I will cite to you, Judge, it doesn't say anything about this particular village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think we dealt with that before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That we'll have to define whether this episode in her statement where the witness says it is -- "That's what I was referring to when I gave my additional comments," that she linked her statement in this respect to the report that was shown to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether that is reliable or not is a matter for us further to consider, whether it is the same. But to put to the witness where she says that it's the same incident, that nothing says if it is the same incident, the statement says something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's not the same incident, then of course the statement doesn't say anything about it. That's the issue which the witness at this moment, I think, cannot clarify any further than what she thinks she is talking about on page 9, second paragraph, and what she thinks the UN document is about, because she considers it to be the same. Otherwise, she wouldn't have taken us to where she said in 1996 so-and-so and so. I think that's the issue which I can't see how the witness can resolve that matter at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes? You would agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, suffice to it to say, Judge --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness -- Madam Witness, when you were given this opportunity in 2007 -- last question. When you were given this in 2007, you said that P10, this report, was accurate, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that question has been put three times now to the witness in different forms. It has been clearly -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also the witness, Mr. Kehoe, to ask a witness whether a report states that a car is green, that's a matter of reading. If a witness would say no, the report says that a car is black, and if we read that it's green, then it doesn't add anything. I mean, what is or what is not in a document is something everyone who can read can establish, and there's no need for the witness to -- I mean, whatever answer she gives, I'll rely upon what I read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I just wanted to bring to your attention the fact that this particular report had in fact been shown to the witness in 2007 and she maintained it was accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. I have nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Then, Witness 136, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you for coming a long way to The Hague and to answer questions of both parties and the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances I would ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom. There's one problem, of course. We have face distortion. So since there's one procedural matter I'd like to deal with for a second, that is the decision on an application for provisional release, if the parties would say it's not a problem that the witness -- it's a public decision anyhow, would stay here, although it doesn't have to do anything with her, but otherwise we have to pull the curtains down and to -- So then we'd like you to stay for a while so that when you leave the courtroom that no one can see you. What we're now dealing with has got nothing to do with you. You are excused, and you are not needed in this courtroom at this moment. Then I would like to inform the -- especially you, Mr. Kay and you, Mr. Cermak, that the Chamber has reached a decision on the application for provisional release. The request is denied. A written decision will be filed this afternoon, but I thought you might want to know, and therefore I thought it the best to inform you right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and it makes a difference to our arrangements in the three weeks. I need to raise a matter in relation to the three-week break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At an early stage of this week, the issue of the disclosure by the Prosecution of the exhibits to be produced through a particular witness was raised. We have now had a week on this trial and we have had experience of dealing with the Rule 65 ter exhibit list as filed by the Prosecutor, as well as starting research on the exhibits connected with witnesses on their witness list which they have served for the first six weeks of trial. We're about to go into a court recess for three weeks. The first witness to be heard next week if the list is maintained in the order that was supplied is a short witness of little consequence, but the witness after that is a substantial witness. His witness statement has within it some 80 attachments. Voluminous documents. It may well be that he's also referred to other documents within the Prosecution 65 ter list. So we could be exceeding this number. In my submission, it is absolutely imperative that we get 14 days' notice of exhibits to be tendered through witnesses before they're called so that we can achieve several things. The first thing is any documents that arise through our research can then be put into the court system through the e-court, and we're then prepared for cross-examination and the Court isn't inconvenienced while we try at late stage to find documents that have to be put into the system to deal with cross-examination of the witness and have only a short period of time in which to do it. The second matter is this: Your Honour, in my view, was rightly concerned with notice given by the Defence of objections to Prosecution evidence. A practice that I'm familiar with that I would see my opponent at the start of a trial, even if a witness was coming up in ten weeks' time or six months' time, give a schedule of objections and say, "Let me know what you think about that," and comment in what's in, and what's out, what we can agree to. Yesterday I served a very brief schedule on Mr. Tieger dealing with the first short witness for our next period in court. I couldn't do that with the witness thereafter at all because I don't know what he's going to produce. Research has to be done as to which of his attachments are within the Rule 65 ter schedule. Your Honour will obviously take notice of the fact that such a schedule is not prepared on a sectioned basis. It is completely random within that schedule as to where a document appears, and so it's very difficult to identify. Nearly 5.000 documents have to be -- go through and linked by ERN to try and find which documents are linked to a particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To achieve good management for Your Honour, and we're concerned to do that, and we have no objection in sending a schedule. If as I understand it and has been reported to me, that the Prosecutor thinks two days before a witness is called is sufficient notice of exhibits to be produced, we will be unable to fulfil Your Honour's intention and neither will we really be adequately prepared in relation to our own documents for cross-examination. These witnesses are scheduled for an hour or two hours because they're 65 ter, so we're likely to be on the same day the witness is called, either the first party for the Defence, second or third, on our feet cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that you want to refer to 92 ter rather than 65 ter where you said these are 65 ter witnesses, but --
